Future Jobs.title: Jobs, Skills and Qualities
Future Jobs.text:
Jobs of the future: data scientist, software developer, renewable energy engineer, drone pilot, robotics engineer, cybersecurity expert, game designer, genetic counsellor.

Skills and qualities: problem-solving, creativity, teamwork, communication, leadership, flexibility, being organised, digital skills, critical thinking.

Language focus, talking about abilities and requirements:
be good at / be skilled at + noun or verb-ing: She is good at solving problems.
be able to + verb: You need to be able to work under pressure.
A pilot needs to have good eyesight.
To be a doctor, you have to study for many years.

Useful phrases: work flexible hours, earn a good salary, have job satisfaction, apply for a job, have an interview, gain experience.
Future Jobs.q: Ayşe wants to be a programmer because she is very good ___ solving puzzles.
Future Jobs.explain: The correct expression is be good at + noun or verb-ing.

Future Jobs.title: Talking About Future Plans
Future Jobs.text:
Language focus, future forms:

be going to: plans and intentions decided before speaking.
I'm going to study engineering at university.
She is going to apply for a summer job.

will: predictions, spontaneous decisions, promises.
I think robots will do many jobs in the future.
The phone is ringing. I'll answer it.

Present continuous: fixed arrangements with a time and place.
I'm meeting the career counsellor at 3 pm tomorrow.

Time expressions: next year, in five years, after graduation, one day, in the future.

Talking about wishes for the future:
I'd like to (would like to) work abroad.
I hope to become a vet.
My dream is to have my own company.
Future Jobs.q: I've already decided. After high school, I ___ study medicine.
Future Jobs.explain: A plan decided before speaking takes be going to + verb: I am going to study.

Hobbies and Skills.title: Hobbies and Free-Time Activities
Hobbies and Skills.text:
Hobbies: playing a musical instrument, painting, photography, coding, gardening, chess, cooking, hiking, collecting stamps, knitting, rock climbing, ebru (paper marbling).

Language focus, expressing likes and dislikes with gerunds (verb-ing):
love, like, enjoy, prefer, don't mind, can't stand, hate + verb-ing
I enjoy taking photos of nature.
My brother can't stand waiting in queues.
She doesn't mind cooking for the family.

Gerunds can also be the subject of a sentence:
Swimming is good for your health.
Learning a new language takes time.

Preposition + verb-ing:
I'm interested in learning the guitar.
He is fond of drawing cartoons.
Hobbies and Skills.q: My grandfather enjoys ___ in his garden every morning.
Hobbies and Skills.explain: After enjoy we use a gerund (verb-ing): enjoys working.

Hobbies and Skills.title: Talking About Experiences
Hobbies and Skills.text:
Language focus, present perfect for experiences:
have / has + past participle (V3)
I have tried rock climbing.
She has never played the violin.
Have you ever been to a pottery workshop? Yes, I have. / No, I haven't.

ever: in questions (at any time in your life)
never: in negative meaning (not at any time)
already, just, yet:
I have just finished my painting.
Have you finished your model yet? Not yet.

Present perfect vs past simple:
I have visited the Istanbul Modern Museum. (experience, no time given)
I visited it last summer. (specific past time → past simple)

for and since:
I have played chess for five years. / since 2020.
Hobbies and Skills.q: Have you ___ tried making ebru (paper marbling)?
Hobbies and Skills.explain: In present perfect questions about life experiences we use ever: Have you ever tried ...?

Hard Times.title: Difficult Times and Disasters
Hard Times.text:
Vocabulary for hard times: earthquake, flood, wildfire, drought, war, refugee, survivor, rescue team, shelter, injured, homeless, damage, collapse, evacuate, donate.

People's reactions: frightened, shocked, devastated, relieved, grateful, brave, hopeful.

Language focus, past continuous:
was / were + verb-ing
It describes an action in progress at a certain time in the past.
At 4 am, most people were sleeping.
What were you doing when the lights went out?

The past continuous often sets the background of a story:
It was raining and the wind was blowing hard.
Hard Times.q: At midnight last night, my parents ___ when the storm started.
Hard Times.explain: An action in progress at a specific time in the past takes the past continuous. My parents (they) were sleeping.

Hard Times.title: Past Continuous and Past Simple: when and while
Hard Times.text:
We use the past continuous and past simple together when a longer action is interrupted by a shorter action.

when + past simple (short action):
I was walking home when the earthquake started.

while + past continuous (long action):
While I was walking home, the earthquake started.

Two long actions happening at the same time:
While the rescue team was searching the building, the volunteers were preparing food.

Sequence of short actions (past simple):
The alarm rang, everyone left the building and went to the assembly area.

Punctuation: When the clause with when / while comes first, we use a comma.
Hard Times.q: The firefighters arrived ___ the people were leaving the building.
Hard Times.explain: The clause after the gap is in the past continuous (were leaving), so we use while.

What a Life.title: Life Stories and Biographies
What a Life.text:
Life events: be born, grow up, go to school, graduate, get a job, get married, have children, retire, become famous, win an award, pass away.

Famous life stories: Aziz Sancar (Nobel Prize in Chemistry, 2015), Marie Curie (two Nobel Prizes), Mimar Sinan (architect), Helen Keller (overcame blindness and deafness), Cahit Arf (mathematician).

Language focus, past simple for finished events in a biography:
Aziz Sancar was born in Savur, Mardin, in 1946.
He studied medicine in Istanbul.
He won the Nobel Prize in 2015.
She didn't give up.

Time linkers in stories: first, then, after that, later, eventually, finally, at the age of 20, in 1990, after graduating.
What a Life.q: Aziz Sancar ___ the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2015.
What a Life.explain: A finished action at a specific time in the past (in 2015): past simple, won.

What a Life.title: Past Perfect
What a Life.text:
Language focus, past perfect:
had + past participle (V3)
We use it for an action that happened before another action in the past.

When I arrived at the station, the train had already left.
(First the train left, then I arrived.)

By the age of 20, she had written two novels.
He had never seen the sea before he moved to Izmir.
Had you finished your homework before the film started?

Compare:
When I got home, my sister cooked dinner. (I arrived, then she cooked.)
When I got home, my sister had cooked dinner. (She cooked before I arrived.)

Useful words: already, before, after, by the time, never ... before.
What a Life.q: By the time the doctor arrived, the patient ___ better.
What a Life.explain: The patient felt better before the doctor arrived: the earlier past action takes the past perfect (had felt).

Back to the Past.title: Past Habits with used to
Back to the Past.text:
Life in the past was different: no internet, no mobile phones, letters instead of messages, black and white TV, fewer cars, playing in the street.

Language focus, used to + base verb:
used to describes past habits or states that are no longer true.
My grandmother used to wash clothes by hand.
People used to write letters to each other.
Children didn't use to have smartphones.
Did you use to play hopscotch?

would can also describe repeated past actions (not states):
Every summer, we would visit our grandparents in the village.

Don't confuse:
used to do (past habit)
be used to doing (be accustomed to): I'm used to getting up early.
Back to the Past.q: When my father was young, there ___ be a cinema in our neighbourhood, but now it is a supermarket.
Back to the Past.explain: A past state that is no longer true: used to + base verb.

Back to the Past.title: Regrets and Wishes About the Past
Back to the Past.text:
Language focus, wish and if only for regrets about the past:
wish + past perfect
I wish I had listened to my grandmother's stories more carefully.
(I didn't listen carefully, and now I regret it.)
If only I had taken more photos of our old house!

wish + past simple for present situations we want to change:
I wish I lived in a quieter place.
I wish I knew how to play the bağlama.

Third conditional for imaginary past situations:
If + past perfect, would have + V3
If I had studied harder, I would have passed the exam.

These structures are useful when talking about history, memories and life lessons.
Back to the Past.q: I didn't visit the old castle when I was in Bursa. Now I regret it. I wish I ___ it.
Back to the Past.explain: A regret about the past takes wish + past perfect: I wish I had visited it.

Open Your Heart.title: Expressing Feelings
Open Your Heart.text:
Feelings: happy, upset, disappointed, frustrated, anxious, embarrassed, jealous, lonely, proud, grateful, confused, excited.

-ed and -ing adjectives:
-ed describes how a person feels: I was bored during the film.
-ing describes the thing that causes the feeling: The film was boring.
excited / exciting, interested / interesting, disappointed / disappointing, tired / tiring

Talking about feelings:
I feel a bit down today.
It makes me happy when people help each other.
I'm worried about my exam results.

Showing empathy:
I'm sorry to hear that.
That must be really hard for you.
I know how you feel.
Don't worry, everything will be fine.
Open Your Heart.q: The ending of the book was very ___. I expected something better.
Open Your Heart.explain: The ending causes the feeling, so we use the -ing adjective: disappointing.

Open Your Heart.title: Apologising, Requests and Giving Advice
Open Your Heart.text:
Apologising:
I'm really sorry. It was my fault.
I apologise for being late.
I didn't mean to hurt your feelings.
Responses: That's OK. / Never mind. / Don't worry about it.

Making polite requests:
Could you help me, please?
Would you mind lending me your notes? (would you mind + verb-ing)
Do you mind if I open the window?

Giving advice:
You should talk to her.
You'd better (had better) apologise.
If I were you, I would tell the truth.
Why don't you write her a letter?

Language focus: Would you mind + verb-ing
Would you mind closing the door? (Please close the door.)
Answer: No, not at all. (= I will do it.)
Open Your Heart.q: Would you mind ___ a little quieter? I'm trying to study.
Open Your Heart.explain: After Would you mind we use verb-ing: Would you mind speaking ...?

Facts About Turkey.title: Places and Facts About Türkiye
Facts About Turkey.text:
Famous places in Türkiye:
Cappadocia: fairy chimneys and hot-air balloons.
Pamukkale: white travertine terraces.
Ephesus: an ancient Roman city.
Göbeklitepe: the oldest known temple in the world.
Mount Nemrut: giant stone heads.
Safranbolu: traditional Ottoman houses.
The Hagia Sophia and the Blue Mosque in Istanbul.

Facts: Türkiye is a bridge between Europe and Asia. It is surrounded by seas on three sides. It is famous for hazelnuts, apricots, figs and tea.

Language focus, superlatives and facts:
Mount Ağrı is the highest mountain in Türkiye.
Lake Van is the largest lake in the country.
The Kızılırmak is the longest river that flows within Türkiye.
Facts About Turkey.q: Lake Van is ___ lake in Türkiye.
Facts About Turkey.explain: Comparing one lake with all the others: superlative, the largest.

Facts About Turkey.title: The Passive Voice
Facts About Turkey.text:
We use the passive when the action or the object is more important than the person who does the action, or when we don't know who did it.

Form: be + past participle (V3)
Present simple passive: am / is / are + V3
Tea is grown in Rize.
Turkish delight is made from sugar and starch.
Past simple passive: was / were + V3
The Hagia Sophia was built in the 6th century.
The Selimiye Mosque was designed by Mimar Sinan.

by + agent shows who did the action (only when it is important).

Active → passive:
Mimar Sinan built the Süleymaniye Mosque.
→ The Süleymaniye Mosque was built by Mimar Sinan.

Negative and question: The bridge wasn't finished on time. Where is hazelnut grown?
Facts About Turkey.explain: The building is the subject and the action is in the past: past simple passive, was built.

Sports.title: Sports and Equipment
Sports.text:
Sports: football, basketball, volleyball, tennis, wrestling, archery, swimming, skiing, cycling, athletics, gymnastics, cirit (a traditional Turkish horse sport).

Equipment: ball, racket, net, goal, bow and arrow, helmet, skis, gloves, whistle.
Places: stadium, court, pitch, pool, track, ring, slope.
People: athlete, coach, referee, team captain, fan, champion.

Famous Turkish athletes: the national women's volleyball team (Filenin Sultanları), Mete Gazoz (archery, Olympic champion), Naim Süleymanoğlu (weightlifting), Busenaz Sürmeneli (boxing).

Language focus, play / go / do with sports:
play + ball games: play volleyball
go + -ing sports: go skiing
do + individual sports and martial arts: do athletics, do taekwondo
Sports.q: Mete Gazoz won an Olympic gold medal in ___.
Sports.explain: Mete Gazoz is an Olympic champion in archery (Tokyo 2020).

Sports.title: Rules and Obligations in Sports
Sports.text:
Language focus, modals for rules and obligation:
must / have to: something is necessary.
Players have to wear helmets in cycling races.
You must stay behind the line.

mustn't: something is not allowed (prohibition).
In football, players mustn't touch the ball with their hands (except the goalkeeper).

don't have to: something is not necessary (but you can if you want).
You don't have to be tall to play football.

can / can't: permission.
In basketball, you can't walk with the ball without dribbling.

Imperatives for instructions:
Keep your back straight. Don't bend your knees.

Careful: mustn't and don't have to have very different meanings!
Sports.q: In volleyball, players ___ catch or hold the ball. It's against the rules.
Sports.explain: Something not allowed by the rules is expressed with mustn't.

My Friends.title: Describing Friends and Friendship
My Friends.text:
Qualities of a good friend: loyal, trustworthy, supportive, honest, understanding, generous, easy-going, sense of humour.

Phrasal verbs about friendship:
get on (well) with: have a good relationship with
fall out with: argue and stop being friends
make up: become friends again after an argument
look up to: admire
rely on / count on: trust someone to help you
hang out: spend time together

Language focus, describing personality:
She's the kind of person who always helps others.
He is someone you can trust.
What I like most about her is her honesty.
My Friends.q: Elif and Deniz had an argument last week, but they ___ yesterday and now they are friends again.
My Friends.explain: To become friends again after an argument is make up; past simple: made up.

My Friends.title: Relative Clauses
My Friends.text:
Relative clauses give more information about a noun. They make descriptions more detailed.

who: for people
A true friend is someone who listens to you.
which: for things and animals
This is the book which my friend gave me.
that: for people or things (in defining clauses)
She's the girl that sits next to me.
whose: for possession
My friend, whose father is a pilot, has visited many countries.
where: for places
This is the café where we usually meet.

Defining relative clauses identify the noun and have no commas.
Non-defining relative clauses give extra information and use commas:
Ali, who lives next door, is my best friend.
My Friends.q: Mert is the friend ___ brother plays in the national basketball team.
My Friends.explain: We need a word that shows possession (Mert's brother): whose.

Values and Norms.title: Values, Norms and Cultures
Values and Norms.text:
Values are ideas that a society believes are important: respect, honesty, tolerance, responsibility, hospitality, justice, solidarity, kindness.

Norms are the unwritten rules of behaviour in a society, and they can be different in different cultures:
In Türkiye, people take off their shoes when they enter a home and kiss the hands of elderly relatives during bayram.
In Japan, people bow to greet each other.
In many countries, it's polite to be on time.

Language focus, it is + adjective + to infinitive:
It is polite to greet your neighbours.
It is rude to interrupt someone.
It's important to respect elderly people.
It is common to give tips in restaurants in the USA.
Values and Norms.q: In Türkiye, ___ to take off your shoes when you enter someone's home.
Values and Norms.explain: The structure is it + be + adjective + to infinitive: It is polite to take off your shoes.

Values and Norms.title: Giving Advice and Expressing Expectations
Values and Norms.text:
Language focus, modals for advice and expectations:

should / ought to: advice, what is right.
You should respect other people's opinions.
We ought to help people in need.

had better: strong advice (or there will be a problem).
You'd better not be late for the meeting.

be supposed to: what is expected by rules or customs.
Guests are supposed to bring a small gift when they visit someone for the first time.
You're not supposed to use your phone during the ceremony.

shouldn't: advice against something.
You shouldn't speak loudly in a library.

After should, ought to and had better we use the base form of the verb.
Values and Norms.q: In our culture, younger people ___ stand up when an elderly person enters the room.
Values and Norms.explain: What is expected by custom is expressed with be supposed to + base verb.
